summary: Three small corrections: I cut an unsupported '1920s and 1930s' date for Benford's work, softened 'Pinkham showed' to 'Pinkham argued' (his uniqueness argument was later found flawed and properly proved by Hill), and fixed a sum (1881 to 1920 is 39 years, not 38). Everything else, including Newcomb's quotations and the Arizona cheques, checked out.

changes.why: No source I found dates Benford's data-gathering to the 1920s; sources say only that he spent years collecting data before publishing in 1938.

changes.before: Pinkham showed that Benford's distribution is scale-invariant
changes.after: Pinkham argued that Benford's distribution is scale-invariant
changes.why: Berger and Hill note that Pinkham's uniqueness argument rested on a flawed assumption (pointed out by Knuth and Raimi); the first correct proof came from Hill. 'Argued' is accurate and fits the next paragraph's 'firmer footing'.

changes.before: first cited in 1920, 38 years after it appeared
changes.after: first cited in 1920, nearly 40 years after it appeared
changes.why: Mir and Ausloos say '38 years', but 1881 to 1920 is 39; 'nearly 40' is true either way.

notes: Mir and Ausloos name Hill (1995) alone as the 'prince' who woke both papers; Nigrini (1996) coincided with the rise in citations and is credited with the first practical application, but did not cite Newcomb. The story's wording is supported by their section 4.
The Hill link is a preprint copy at williams.edu rather than the American Scientist page; its text matches the 1998 article (DOI 10.1511/1998.4.358 confirmed via benfordonline.net).
Benford's '20 lists' is confirmed by Hill (1995, Statistical Science: '20 different tables') and the 20,229 total by Hill (1998) and Leemis et al. (2000).
The further-reading link is the same Newcomb PDF as the first source; counted as a separate link check.
